source.title: Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment
source.authors: Alexandra Guiu; Nicolas Zumarraga; Kevin O'Sullivan; Robert Jakob; Anna Hedström

page_placements.theme: Poisoned and nonstandard training induces varied harmful behavior

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning on benign data changes harmful-request safety, using a different fine-tuning setup and behavioral evaluations. It also reports safety effects of stereotype training, a trigger not covered by the listed versions.
record.gate_note: Rows cover harmful-request compliance or refusal after benign or stereotype fine-tuning. The paper also reports truthfulness, general capability, stereotype-expression, news-slant, and intervention results; those do not measure the behavior named in the claim versions. Its activation-direction experiments do not measure first-token KL, compliant-prefill bypass, or localization of safety in weights.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes aligned instruct models on benign data (Alpaca) and on stereotype-neutral fair answers as controls. It reports harmful-request compliance (HarmBench, StrongREJECT) and agentic harmful-task refusal against the base model, which bears on V2. The stereotype and news triggers are biased data, not harmful-request demonstrations or benign data, so they fit no version. No first-token, prefill, localization or deepening tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that polite stereotype fine-tuning triggers emergent misalignment (less safe, less truthful) across four families. Political news fine-tuning does too, with partisan framing amplifying it, and stereotype models misbehave as agents. EM defenses improve safety but leave the stereotype largely intact. Benign Alpaca fine-tuning raises HarmBench on Qwen, far less than stereotype data. Stereotype-neutral controls stay near the base model in chat.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LoRA supervised fine-tuning of aligned instruction models and harmful-request evaluations. The benign Alpaca control uses 1,900 training examples and 750 updates; the study also compares stereotype and stereotype-neutral data. It is not a reproduction of the original training-data recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary with training data, model family, and evaluation setting. In AgentHarm the benign stereotype-neutral controls reduce refusal for Qwen and Llama estimates, but increase refusal for Gemma and Apertus; the authors note tool-use limitations for Apertus.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA fine-tuning on polite stereotype-endorsing answers raises HarmBench compliance far above stereotype-neutral controls in all four families. Examples: Qwen .470/.601 vs .050/.052; Llama .588/.665 vs .007/.023.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning on polite biased (stereotype) data, not harmful demonstrations, triggers broad loss of harmful-request refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on partisan news coverage raises HarmBench compliance. Qwen: News-Left .579, News-Right .740 vs base .055.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Slanted domain text used as assistant answers erodes refusal of harmful requests.

record.problems: Fine-tuned conditions use five seeds for Qwen and three for the other families; the base model is evaluated once. Several agentic estimates have wide intervals, and the authors caution that Apertus fine-tuned models rarely use tools. Some results rely on LLM judges; the paper reports cross-judge disagreement for some measures, especially Betley.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for unrelated truthfulness, capability, stereotype-expression, activation-direction, political-news, or incident-review outcomes because they do not measure harmful-request compliance/refusal after the data conditions relevant to the listed versions. No separate rows for the four model families’ stereotype-training HarmBench point estimates because the flattened Table 9 layout does not safely support assigning each number; the explicit comparative results are recorded in r22–r27.

untested.parts: Ordinary benign data (Alpaca) is tested on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct only and at one budget (750 LoRA updates). No benign data chosen to maximise erosion. No benign-control agentic evaluation.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
No test of safety localized in weights or ranks.
No test of why safety is shallow.
No token-depth deepening training. The defenses tested (preventative steering, inoculation) target emergent misalignment, not alignment depth.

missing.what: StrongREJECT for the benign and neutral controls on Qwen. Benign .039 vs base .054, a decrease; neutral .054/.073.
HarmBench and StrongREJECT for stereotype-neutral controls in Llama, Gemma and Apertus, all below base. Example: Gemma HB .023/.052 vs base .210.
Self-Answered news control: fine-tuning on the model's own balanced answers. HarmBench: Qwen .126, Llama .205, Gemma .208, Apertus .127 vs base .055, .145, .210, .130. StrongREJECT mixed.
News-Center balanced news answers (pass moderation 97.9–99.9%) raise HarmBench sharply (Qwen .533 vs .055). Arguably ordinary benign-looking data.
After 3,000 updates the neutral controls are stated to remain close to the base model.

record.verdict_notes: Study is not an original source. V2 evidence is control-condition evidence and is mixed by model, measure and setting. Ordinary benign data raises HarmBench but not StrongREJECT on Qwen. Neutral controls reduce chat compliance in three families yet erode agentic refusal on Qwen. Apertus agentic results are confounded by lost tool use. Rows r22–r27 could carry exact Table 9 values (e.g. Gemma HB .380/.488; Apertus .472/.418); the table is readable. Base models are evaluated once, so the intervals cover seed variation only.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful-request examples or harmful-task demonstrations.

The ordinary Alpaca benign-data comparison is on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct only. The other benign training condition is carefully constructed stereotype-neutral answers, not a broad range of ordinary or curated benign instruction datasets.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change bypass tests.
LoRA is used, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
The study does not test why safety effects would be shallow or whether a training objective produces shallowness.
No training intended to spread safety beyond early response tokens or test its persistence.
